title: Leaderless Replication
summary:
In leaderless replication **every replica of a key can accept reads and writes**, and nobody orders writes. Whichever node receives a client request acts as that request's **coordinator** (not a leader) and talks to the key's replicas.

Think of an engineering team serving customers: each engineer is assigned to different customers, yet every change (a feature, a fix) ends up in the same shared service, and eventually everyone learns what happened.

Structure (Dynamo / Cassandra style):

```
Key -> hash -> Partition -> Replica set [A, B, C]   (replication factor N = 3)
Client -> any node = coordinator for this request -> replicas
```

- A write succeeds when **W** replicas confirm; a read consults **R** replicas and reconciles. See the [write path](#/sd/f/leaderless-write-path), the [read path](#/sd/f/leaderless-read-path), [quorum](#/sd/f/leaderless-quorum) and [repair](#/sd/f/leaderless-repair).
- **No failover:** a down replica just means fewer acks, so availability is high.
- **Costs:** replicas may disagree, so every value needs version metadata; concurrent writes can conflict; and there is no global order or transaction across keys.

Use it for high availability and write throughput on key-addressed data that tolerates eventual convergence (shopping carts, sessions, time series, activity feeds). Avoid it where an invariant needs a single arbiter (balances, uniqueness) unless you add consensus. Contrast with [leader-based replication](#/sd/f/leader-based-replication).

drills.q: A replica set of three loses one node. What does a client writing at W = 2 see in a leaderless system, compared with the same loss being the leader in a single-leader system?
options: Leaderless: the write still succeeds with 2 acks. Single-leader: writes pause until failover completes
drills.explain: No node is special, so losing one only reduces the available acks. Losing the leader removes the only place that accepts writes until a new one is chosen.

drills.q: Node X coordinates client 1's write of key K, and node Y coordinates client 2's write of K at the same moment. What is true in a leaderless system?
options: Replicas may apply the two writes in different orders, so versions must be compared to decide the outcome
X is the leader for K, so its write wins
The replicas lock K to serialise them
Y's write is rejected because X coordinated first
drills.explain: A coordinator only drives one request; it has no authority over the key. Without a single orderer, concurrency must be resolved with version metadata (timestamps or version vectors).

drills.q: Which workloads fit leaderless replication? Select all that apply.
options: A shopping cart that must always accept adds, even during a partial outage
A uniqueness check for usernames across all users
An inventory counter that must never go below zero
drills.explain: Carts and sessions prefer availability and can merge or overwrite. Uniqueness and non-negative invariants need an arbiter; with no leader, two writers can both succeed.

drills.q: Order the pieces of a leaderless request path.
items: The client sends the request to any node (the coordinator)
The key is hashed to a partition
The partition maps to its replica set
The coordinator waits for W acks (write) or R responses (read)
drills.explain: Placement is deterministic from the key; only the coordinator is incidental. That is why any node can take any request.

drills.q: A leaderless cluster has 9 nodes and replication factor 3. There is 30 TB of unique data, spread evenly. How much disk does each node use on average, in TB?
drills.explain: Raw data is 30 x 3 = 90 TB; spread over 9 nodes it is 10 TB each. Replication multiplies storage by N, regardless of whether there is a leader.

drills.q: Explain a coordinator in leaderless replication, and why it is not a leader.
drills.answer: The coordinator is whichever node received the request; it fans the operation out to the key's replicas and collects W or R responses. It is chosen per request and holds no authority over ordering, so different requests for the same key can have different coordinators.
